q: Structure A can be found in
n: Structure A is the Ziggurat of Ur, a Sumerian temple tower near Nasiriyah, Iraq. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ur; UNESCO (Ahwar of Southern Iraq).

q: Structure B can be found in
n: Structure B is Stonehenge, near Amesbury, Wiltshire, England. Source: UNESCO (Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites); English Heritage.

q: Structure C can be found in
n: Structure C is El Castillo (Temple of Kukulcán) at Chichén Itzá, Yucatán, Mexico. Source: UNESCO (Pre-Hispanic City of Chichen-Itza).

q: Structure D can be found in
n: Structure D is the Malwiya spiral minaret of Samarra, Iraq. Source: UNESCO (Samarra Archaeological City).

q: Structure E can be found in
n: Structure E is the pyramid group at Giza, Egypt. The pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, with the Sphinx, stand on the Giza plateau west of Cairo. Source: UNESCO (Memphis and its Necropolis).

q: Which megalithic tomb has a central chamber ringed by smaller side chambers?
n: A passage tomb has a central chamber, often cruciform with smaller side chambers, reached by a long passage under a mound, as at Newgrange. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, passage grave; Fletcher.

q: Which prehistoric structure is a ring of upright stones carrying horizontal slabs?
n: A stone circle is a ring of standing stones. At Stonehenge the uprights carry horizontal lintels (trilithons). Source: English Heritage (Stonehenge); Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which early dwelling was made of tree branches covered with turf?
n: The hut, a frame of tree branches covered with turf, hide or thatch, was one of the earliest freestanding human dwellings. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Kostof, A History of Architecture.

q: Which shelter leans one side against a cave, with stones at its base?
n: A lean-to is a simple shelter with one sloping side propped against a support such as a cave wall, its base held down with stones. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Ching.

q: The Great Ziggurat of Ur belongs to which architecture?
n: The Great Ziggurat of Ur (about 2100 BC, built by Ur-Nammu) is Sumerian architecture. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ur; Fletcher.

q: Mesopotamia, where architecture first developed, is mostly in which present-day country?
n: Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates, lies mostly in present-day Iraq. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mesopotamia.

q: What was the main building material of Sumerian architecture?
n: Sumerian architecture was built mainly of sun-dried mud brick, with fired brick for facings. Stone and timber were scarce in the river plain. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What are the principal monuments of prehistoric architecture?
n: The principal surviving monuments of prehistoric architecture are tombs and burial monuments (dolmens, passage graves, tumuli). Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Mesopotamia is known for which structure?
n: Mesopotamia is known for the ziggurat, a stepped temple tower of mud brick topped by a shrine. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, ziggurat.

q: Where are the Tarxien Temples?
n: The Tarxien Temples (about 3150–2500 BC) are a megalithic temple complex on Malta. Source: UNESCO (Megalithic Temples of Malta).

q: Where are the Olmec colossal heads?
n: The Olmec colossal heads are on Mexico's Gulf Coast, at San Lorenzo and La Venta. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Olmec.

q: Where are the nuraghe towers?
n: Nuraghi are Bronze Age stone towers found in Sardinia, Italy, such as Su Nuraxi at Barumini. Source: UNESCO (Su Nuraxi di Barumini).

q: Where is Göbekli Tepe?
n: Göbekli Tepe (about 9500 BC) is in southeastern Anatolia, Turkey. Its carved T-shaped pillars, about 11,000 years old, are among the oldest known monumental structures. Source: UNESCO (Göbekli Tepe).

q: Where are the Callanish Stones?
n: The Callanish (Calanais) Stones are on the Isle of Lewis, Outer Hebrides, Scotland. Source: Historic Environment Scotland.

q: Which burial mound has a long, narrow passage and a gallery?
n: A passage tomb is a burial mound with a long, narrow stone passage and gallery leading to the burial chamber. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, passage grave.

q: Which burial place runs north–south, with a long narrow path leading to an open court?
n: A court tomb (court cairn) has an open forecourt in front of a long gallery, often aligned roughly east–west or north–south. It is common in northern Ireland. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, megalith; Irish National Monuments Service.

q: Which tomb is roofed by slabs laid directly on its side walls, often with outer rows of walling?
n: A wedge tomb is roofed by slabs laid directly on its side walls. It narrows and lowers toward the back and often has outer walling. Source: Irish National Monuments Service; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Which shelter leans on one side of a cave, propped on rows of supports?
n: A lean-to leans one side against a cave wall or other support, with its sloping roof propped on rows of supports. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Which early dwelling of wooden twigs stood on plains or cliffs?
n: The hut, made of wooden twigs or branches, was the first freestanding shelter, built on plains or cliff edges. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Which prehistoric tomb has upright stones capped by one large flat slab?
n: A dolmen is a prehistoric tomb of upright stones capped by one large flat slab, like a stone table. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What is a circle of large stones enclosing a monument or burial mound?
n: A cromlech is a circle of large standing stones, often enclosing a mound or monument. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What is a single tall standing stone of ritual meaning?
n: A menhir ("long stone" in Breton) is a single tall upright standing stone of ritual meaning. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What is a prehistoric mound of earth and stones over one or more graves?
n: A tumulus (barrow) is a prehistoric mound of earth and stones over one or more graves. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What is any structure of large stones, usually set without mortar, for ritual or burial?
n: A megalith is any structure of large stones, usually set without mortar, for ritual or burial: dolmens, menhirs, cromlechs. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Item A is called:
n: Item A is the cornice, the uppermost projecting part of a classical entablature, which crowns the wall and throws rainwater clear of it. The architrave is the lowest part and the frieze the middle. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.
